newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-MUTTERINGS BEYOND THE BOUNDARY LINE.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-MUTTERINGS BEYOND THE BOUNDARY LINE.

text.p: The muted thud of ball on bat has been joined by a new sound at English county cricket grounds this season.

Not the gentle clinking of beer glasses in the members' bar or the re-arranging of deckchairs by straw-hatted septuagenarians but mutterings of discontent from one of the quieter corners of the field.
The humble scorers, unassuming and often unpaid men in striped ties and county blazers, are nursing a grievance out beyond the boundary line.
If some newspaper headlines are to be believed, the cathedral city calm of English county cricket could next month be jolted by its first strike in 130 years.

"There is anger, frustration and resentment that the England and Wales Cricket Board are running roughshod over us," Surrey scorer Keith Booth was quoted as saying in the Daily Telegraph newspaper last week.

"Scoreboard serfs ready for rebellion," declared the Guardian's Paul Weaver, relishing the prospect of the day when the scorer "tweaked his rubber eraser menacingly, sharpened his stubby pencil and marched to war."

While one or two retired colonels in the home counties may have been spluttering into their breakfast cereal or firing off angry correspondence about the reports, the reality is somewhat The Association of County Cricket Scorers (ACCS), grouping 36 first and second team scorers from the 18 counties, have called an extraordinary general meeting in Derby on Monday to air their grievances.

"The real reason for the meeting is that the scorers are dissatisfied with the re-appointment of the television scorer Malcolm Ashton for the tour of the West Indies," ACCS chairman Ted Lester told Reuters.
Ashton, considerably younger than most county scorers who are sometimes paid no more than expenses and often drawn from the ranks of retired accountants and bankers, is not a member of the ACCS.
"I assume a motion will be put to the meeting to propose a strike," said Lester, a former Yorkshire scorer. "There are one or two who would like to see a strike taking place."
But he declined to identify the proposer "in case it gets him into bother with his county."
He also acknowledged that the likelihood of any action beyond a formal complaint looked remote, mainly because most scorers were worried about their jobs.
The other is that, in a sport where good form is as important as keeping a straight bat and one's eye on the ball, a strike is "simply not cricket".
The scorers feel they are being ignored by the English Cricket Board (ECB) and want the prestigious job of tour scorer to be shared among their members.
"The scorers feel it's an honour to score for England and having scored at county level, they should have the chance to go one step up," Lester said.
They also feel that they have handled the introduction of computer technology at county level and not been rewarded for their efforts by the ECB.
Any strike would also only affect the ACCS and not the unrelated Association of Cricket Umpires and Scorers (ACUS), which is not involved.
Some scorers are also aghast at the strike threat, with Hampshire's Vic Isaacs staunchly opposed.
"It's a dreadful idea. You won't find me with a placard outside Lord's," he said last week.
Clem Driver, the 70-something Essex scorer, was also clearly in the anti-strike camp.
"I think in fact that the movers of the motion would do best without my presence," he wrote to Lester.
"I am very much against futile gestures of any sort as I believe they weaken any case one is promoting.

"I have nothing whatever against Mr Ashton...but have always made public my view that it is a pity to have broken the tradition that the undoubted 'perk' be offered to a suitable county scorer," Driver added.

His Worcestershire counterpart, 75-year-old Jim Sewter, said he shared Driver's viewpoint. Both men chatted affably as they watched their counties prepare for battle in a county match at the Essex ground.
Both also agreed however that the traditional job of scorer has changed considerably in their time.
In the distant past, a scorer's most valuable piece of equipment was a trusty pocket knife to record the runs by carving notches in a handy hazel stick.
Written scoresheets and ledgers emerged in the 19th century and laptop computers in the last decade.
The computer technology and complex calculations needed in one-day matches in the event of rain stopping play have driven some of the scorers away.

"One or two felt they couldn't do it and had to give up, which is sad, very sad," said Driver, who professed himself happy enough with the computer equipment after overcoming some initial reservations.
"It didn't inspire too much confidence at first when you turned the thing on and it said University of California or somewhere on it," he said.
"One wonders how much they know about cricket."
